newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel split on Baxter stem cell device.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel split on Baxter stem cell device.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel on Thursday was split on whether Baxter Healthcare Corp's Isolex 300, a stem cell separation system, benefits patients.
The panel voted six to five, with five abstentions, that the data presented by Baxter, a unit of Baxter International, failed to prove efficacy.

The device, which pulls healthy cells out of a patient's own blood and purges tumor cells, did produce cells appropriate for re-infusion, but so do procedures that don't use the Isolex, said the committee.
The panel did not make a formal recommendation for or against approval, leaving it to the agency to decide.
However, most of the panel said there were too few patients -- only about 40 were studied -- to judge the device's true value. Some felt it had no utility.
"I don't think any clinical benefit has been shown," said Dr. Virginia Broudy, of the University of Washington school of medicine.
The committee recommended that Baxter conduct another large trial to prove efficacy.
Baxter said its studies showed that the Isolex allowed cancer patients to receive tumor cell-free autologous blood transplants and that it promoted growth of healthy cells.

The FDA let Baxter, which applied for approval in February 1997, present early, phase I/II data. But the agency criticized the firm's study design, and also noted that tumor cells were reduced, but were still detected in blood prepared for reinfusion using the Baxter device.
The FDA said the death rate was slightly higher in patients getting the Isolex-selected blood -- 11 deaths in a year -- compared to seven in the other group.

Baxter said that 24 patients receiving Isolex-selected cells produced new white blood cells within 11 days, compared to 10 days for the 24 patients who received transplants without the Baxter system. It took 12 days for new platelets to form with the Baxter system, compared to 10 for the non-device group.

The difference was not statistically significant, showing there was no real difference between success of transplants aided by the device or without the Isolex. That led panelists to question whether the device had any benefit.
A similar device was approved by the FDA in December 1996, but only for autologous bone marrow transplantation. Baxter sued that manufacturer, CellPro, for patent infringement in 1995.
In March of this year a Delaware jury awarded Baxter $2.3 million. On Thursday, the judge ordered CellPro to pay treble damages and legal fees.
The court has also said CellPro can continue selling its device until Baxter's device is approved. CellPro has appealed that ruling.
